title: A message stick collected by Neil Hamilton Fairley, possibly from near Cairns
description: Kirsten Palmer wrote on 18.01.2025: "Dear Dr Piers Kelly  My name is Kirsten Palmer and I have been advised to contact you with regards this map stick.  I have have always understood that this was used to guide Aboriginal tribes from one encampment to another, left there for the return journeys. I inherited this from my father, we used to have quite a large collection of Aboriginal artefacts at home.    The reason for this is that my maiden name is Hamilton Fairley. My grandfather (who was an Australian ) Sir Neil Hamilton Fairley, was a Professor of Tropical Diseases. He did all the work on Malaria in the Second World War, coming up with a cure thus saving thousand of soldiers lives in the Middle East.    He worked from Cains , in the military museum in Canberra there is a whole section devoted to the work he did. Sir William Dargie, was a close personal friend of my grand parents, William, was the official Artist and accompanied my grandfather to Papua New Guinea.    During the war years my father went to Geelong and staying in Corowa with an uncle. My Grand mother bought a house in Melbourne.  My father told me how to read the stick and as I’m dyslexic I totally equate with visual representation for navigation.    I also know that my grand father had a close colleague, who , in the 1920’s lived with a tribe, who allowed him to document and photograph the everyday life and rituals of the people. There was a small typed book , illustrated with black and white photos, unfortunately after my father died I could not find it anywhere, hopefully my father did the right thing and sent it to the right place in Australia. The impression that I got was that this stick comes from that research.    I am well aware that this is a precious artefact and should be some where it will be valued. I have always looked after it well ,keeping it at a reasonable temperature.    Could you advise me the right way to get this to the right place.  I look forward to hearing from you.  Best regards  Kirsten"
note_place_created: This is a terminus ante quem: it is the date that Fairley established the malaria research unit in Cairns but note that if it had been acquired from his colleague in the 1920s it could be earlier.

title: A message stick made by Mawalan 1 Marika inviting the djunggayi of the Yirritja moiety to attend the Djang'kawu (goanna) ceremony
description: Message stick. Physical Description: Rectangular message stick with 'handles' on either end - a smaller width, and no carving. Both faces are slightly convex towards the lateral edges. All faces, including lateral edges, are carved - a banded pattern of small squares on the faces, and squares and chevrons on the lateral edges. title: A message stick from Mornington Island held in the University of Queensland Anthropology Museum
description: Message stick. Physical Description: Object a medium hardwood and is rectangular with four lateral surfaces. Three of the surfaces have vertical lines etched into the wood and on the fourth is a zig zag pattern.  There are chevrons on two of the surfaces. The etchings are coloured a red paint and the object overall has been painted a browny/red colour. Registration number is inscribed in black.
notes_ling_area: The origin of the message stick is Mornington Island, Gulf region, Queensland, Australia
message: The donor recorded that the markings announced an initiation ceremony.  Parallel strokes on two sides refer to the groups involved: people at the mission camp; Denham Island; Forsyth Island; Laroombin division and Dugoorabin. The zig zag design is recorded as boomerangs, symbols of authority to communicate the importance of the event [Belcher source file].
collector: Collected and donated by: Reverend Douglas Belcher
file_copyright: The University of Queensland Anthropology Museum
notes_coords: Coordinates for Mornington Island, Queensland, per Google maps
notes: UQ Anthropology Museum website: "The donor recorded that the markings announced an initiation ceremony.  Parallel strokes on two sides refer to the groups involved: people at the mission camp; Denham Island; Forsyth Island; Laroombin division and Dugoorabin. The zig zag design is recorded as boomerangs, symbols of authority to communicate the importance of the event [Belcher source file].    Memmott (1980:131) records the involved groups as people at the mission camp, Yangkal people from Denham Island and Forsyth Island, Larumpenta (division of Lardil) and Tjirrkarampenta division. He also noted that this four-sided stick of milled timber is atypical for the area, two-sided bush timber was more commonly used.    Source: Memmott, Paul 1980 Occasional Papers in Anthropology Vol 9 p107-142"

title: Message Sticks Nanhthi Mak video
description:
Uploaded to YouTube on 5 March 2025.

Description from Wadeye People and Culture: "Message sticks were sent to neighbouring clans to inform them of an upcoming ceremony and to bring some boys for initiation and dancers. The messengers were allowed to travel around freely without danger of attack. When people wanted to visit another clan they lit fires on the way to tell them people were coming for a visit rather than an enemy attack."

00:08: Language Murrin Patha Bring Young Men and People for Dancing at a Ceremony

6:56: CREDITS Cultural Knowledge Holders

Dudhawa Frank Jinjair (Dimgek)

Mayi Nguyngitjinnang Clan

(Wakal Thinang)

Language Djaminjung

Melvuyen Claver Dumoo Wuynbu

Ma Thangarral Lambu Tjendi

Malimandi Rak Yenmungiririni

notes_coords: Absolute coordinates for Wadeye
notes: 22.05.2025 PK: Note that Frank Jinjair is the man left in the headband, and Malviyin Claver Dumoo is on the right, as confirmed by John Mansfield.     Jeff Hardwick contacted PK on 20.05.2025: "Hi Piers, a friend sent me your ABC Radio talk on message sticks. Have always been fascinated by them. Attached a link for a video of these two old men in their 80s at Wadeye. Frank Jinjair who is Murin Kura language from the Fitzmaurice River learnt Djaminjung where he was born on Legune Station. He made these message sticks from Cypress pine. Wonderful. Went to Armidale Teachers College in the 70s. Regards Jeff Hardwick Batchelor NT Watch "Message Sticks Nanhthi Mak" on YouTube"  PK replied on 21.05.2025: "Hi Jeff,  This is absolutely terrific!  Are you able to tell me what date you made this video, or at least what year?  And could I include it in the Australian Message Stick Database?    As it happens I live practically next door to the Armidale Teachers College, which is now the New England Conservatorium of Music but everyone still calls it the Teachers College.   All the best,  Piers"    Jeff Hardwick replied on 21.05.2025: "Thanks glad to hear someone who digs message sticks. Video was recorded on 1st Nov 2015 in Murrin Patha. Also have versions in Djaminjung and Marri Tjevin. Yes put it on the database. Will send some photos on my other email. Please send a link. Have always been interested in totemic designs that have huge cosmic meanings. How indigenous people compressed this into something that looks simple but is not simple but complex. Like to promote Wadeye as too much focus on Arnhem Land.  Cheers Jeff"    PK replied on 21.05.2025: "Hi Jeff,   If these two men are still alive I would love to meet them in Wadeye.   If you're able to send those additional versions in Djaminjug and Marri Tjevin, please do, or add them to YouTube. Please also send the images.     I'm very happy to promote Wadeye and I can send a link when the database is reissued in its updated version. This can take up to 6 months because it's a bit of a technical headache.     All the best,  Piers"  Jeff Hardwick replied on 21.05.2025: "Yes they are still alive but frail. Frank got smashed in the face years ago with a kangaroo jack and damaged nerves. He is a respected lawman. Real old school. Claver is frail but still with it like Frank. He was more a hunter, didge player but very clever craftsman. Most old people gone now.  If you want to go to Wadeye sometime won't be a problem. Have a lot of friends there. We are going to Barunga Festival on 6th June. Driving out to Wadeye in the bush holiday 26th June from Batchelor. Will send other videos later. Photo is my friend Mayili Gregory Munar who is a lawman, frontman for lirrga dance group and TO for his country. Marri Ngarr language. Top culture man. Also ALO police.     Cheers Jeff"    Jeff Harwick replied on 21.05.2025: "The message sticks [attached photographs] are to ask people to come for a boys initiation ceremony. Bring boys for initiation and men and women for dancing. Was thrilled when Frank pulled them out of his bag and gave them to me. Put on database.  Cheers Jeff"

title: Term for 'message stick' in Waanyi
description: Original source gloss (Laughren 2025): diwurrurru  noun. letter stick, message stick. Mudamudajibi yalu jibana. Windijbi nyulu nanangkanyi kundaanyi, diwurrurru-anyi. Windijbi nyulu manii. They wrapped (it) in paperbark. He gave (him) that piece of wood, that message stick to him. He handed it (to him). [RS2005-03] Also pronounced as: diwurruwurru.
notes:
16.06.2025 PK: Mary Laughren shared draft of dictionary with PK 16.06.2025:PK to ML "Thank you so much Mary! The example sentence is very interesting:

Mudamudajibi yalu jibana. Windijbi nyulu nanangkanyi kundaanyi, diwurrurru-anyi. Windijbi nyulu manii. 'They wrapped (it) in paperbark. He gave (him) that piece of wood, that message stick to him. He handed it (to him)'.

The objects discovered at Message Stick Cave were also wrapped in paperbark. Sometimes this sort of thing indicates a restriction – the object cannot be seen. But in other cases, message sticks were wrapped in paperbark simply to carry them and even to make them more visible.

Below is an example of message-stick-carrying device from the National Museum. It was apparently designed to hold a message stick up in order to be seen, and for the messenger's protected status to be assured. Ordinary paper-and-pen letters could also be carried in this way.

Do you happen to know what the Waanyi message stick tradition is? Are there restrictions on seeing the objects? Or is the paperbark more like an envelope?

Many thanks again, Piers

[16.06.2025]: Hi Piers,

I don't really know much about the role of message sticks among Waanyi people. I got the impression from Roy Seccin that they were 'open' objects used to convey information and that they were wrapped up in paperbark. He didn't say why they were wrapped up, and I didn't ask. In the desert people wrapped up stone knives for protection for the objects and also those carrying them.

John Dymock also recorded this word being used for a 'letter'.

Same word in Garrwa.

I've had a further look at my notes following on from the example in the dictionary. Roy explains that they hand the wrapped up message stick to a person to take to where other designated people are —Roy says that the stick is handed to old people who look at it and know what it means. They then gather up their things, specifically weapons and head off to meet up with others —they gather to fight against other people.

I recorded this in March 2005.

It seems odd that information would be sent via a message stick when it could have been delivered orally by the carrier. This makes me think that only some people, e.g., men who had learned to read the symbols as part of male initiation would be able to interpret them (hence the 'old men' (wululuku) in Roy's account. However this is speculation on my part.

Cheers, Mary

title: Two message sticks discovered wrapped in paperbark at Message Stick Cave, Riversleigh Station
description: Michael Archer: "a bundle of artefacts wrapped in paperbark (Melaleuca species of tree) which was tied up with human hair string. The bundle contained two message sticks."
notes_coords: MA: "in the limestone cliffs along the Gregory River in Boodjamulla National Park, Riversleigh Station, northwestern Queensland."  PK: The coordinates here are for the approximate location of Gregory River and not the known location of the cave in the limestone cliffs
notes:
Correspondence with Michael Archer and Henk Godthelp in 2025. 13.06.2025: Dear Michael,

I am a researcher in anthropology at the University of New England. I'm just getting in touch because you mention a site, in a few of your papers, named Message Stick Cave.

Since my major research project is on message sticks, I'm very curious about this site and how it got its name.

Are you able to tell me more? Can you share where precisely this cave is to be found? All the best,

Piers

13.06.2025:

Hi Piers,

Message Stick Cave is a very small cave in the limestone cliffs along the Gregory River in Boodjamulla National Park, Riversleigh Station, northwestern Queensland. One of our palaeontological team members found in this cave a bundle of artefacts wrapped in paperbark (Melaleuca species of tree) which was tied up with human hair string. The bundle contained two message sticks. These were identified as such by Waanyi Nation elders and later repatriated by them to another site known only to them. The precise locality details for the cave cannot be revealed for security reasons.

Hope this helps!

Cheers

Mike

14.06.2025:

Hi all

I am not able to give anything but a ballpark date of 1986 or maybe 87. I left the bundle undisturbed and didn't see the contents, but one of the elders told me they were used when local tribes came together and didn't elaborate any further. He also didn't use a Waanyi word to describe the objects. I was told much later, in 2007 or so, that they were in a keeping place and were known to the current custodians. The topic came up in a discussion with Michael Slack and several of the male elders.

Cheers

Henk

[16.06.25]: Wonderful, thank you Michael and Henk!

Sorry to pester you with a follow-up question: When you described it as a "bundle of artefacts", does that mean there were other objects in the paperbark in addition to the message sticks? As it happens this represents only one of three known cases of message sticks discovered in situ in an archaeological context which is why I'm so keen to know.

Incidentally, the Waanyi term for message stick in Mary Laughren's unpublished dictionary is diwurrurru and she includes an example sentence:

Mudamudajibi yalu jibana. Windijbi nyulu nanangkanyi kundaanyi, diwurrurru-anyi. Windijbi nyulu manii. 'They wrapped (it) in paperbark. He gave (him) that piece of wood, that message stick to him. He handed it (to him).'

This would seem to indicate that wrapping message sticks in paperbark is a known Waanyi practice. There are other places where this happens too, especially in the Top End where paperbark is used to help transport message sticks but not to hide them from, eg, women or uninitiated boys.

Cheers,

Piers [17.06.25]: Hi I didn't see the bundle unwrapped and can only report that the elders talked only of the sticks.

Sorry I be of more assistance there. Message Stick cave was quite close to large well decorated shelter that I was told was an initiation site. 16.06.2025 PK: Consider example sentence for 'message stick' in Mary Laughren's dictionary:

Mudamudajibi yalu jibana. Windijbi nyulu nanangkanyi kundaanyi, diwurrurru-anyi. Windijbi nyulu manii. 'They wrapped (it) in paperbark. He gave (him) that piece of wood, that message stick to him. He handed it (to him)'.

This suggest the paperbark is like a paperbark wallet or paper yabber and not a covering for a restricted object. To follow up with Michael Slack.

title: Three message sticks in the care of Ellen Spalding
notes: [15.06.2025]  :Dear Piers,    I hope this finds you well.    I am writing regarding a collection of three wooden objects that Melanie Raberts from the First People's Department at Museum Victoria has identified in the following way:    "In response to your question about the three beautiful carvings in your family’s care – they are message sticks (as you have already noted).  Caine Muir, Senior Curator and I have compared the carvings with message sticks in the First Peoples Collection and can provenance them to Western Australia, but we would hesitate to further refine the geographic source.  The extremely fine etchings, patterning and the overall shape and polish of the timber are striking."    Melanie did suggest that we get in touch with you in the hope of finding out more.    My late father, Ian Spalding (1928-2019), grew up in the Victorian Western District town of Ararat and these message sticks were in a drawer in the Spalding family home as long as he could remember. This means that their history in our family goes back at least 100 years. Apart from that their provenance is unknown.    I am hoping you might be able to offer further advice to their origin? We are also keen to know if you have any thoughts on repatriating/re-homing them.    My father's sister, Marjorie Glasson, who also grew up with the message sticks, is technically the current 'owner'. Essentially I am contacting you on her behalf and she is enthusiastic about the idea that they might be repatriated or re-homed. Marjorie is also holds our family history knowledge and although she does not know exactly how they came to be in the family I believe she has some ideas about what the Western Australian connection might be. She would be happy to be contacted if it happened that you were interested in any further discussion about their origin.    If you were kind enough to offer your thoughts on these items we would be really grateful.    Many thanks,    Ellen Spalding  Footscray    [18.06.2025:]  Hi Ellen,   So sorry, your message went into my Spam folder for some reason and I've only just discovered it there.    The very fine etching with infilled shapes and polishing is very typical of message sticks from the Murchison district of Western Australia, though this style does seem to pop up occasionally in other places.     These are excellent well-preserved examples and it's clear that you have looked after them in the right conditions.     I would not say that they have greater-than-usual cultural significance and there is nothing about the designs that would indicate that they are sacred or restricted. So if you were to continue to hold onto them in your family for the time being I personally believe that would be acceptable.     But if the traditional owners can be found, there may well be a Keeping Place or similar where they can be safely returned. Without narrower provenance information it might be too tricky to repatriate them. An alternative is to donate them to a museum in Western Australia but they might not accept them without sufficient evidence of their origins.    Please let me know if there are any stories in your family history that might link them to a specific locale, or family.     In the meantime, if you agree, I can add them to the Australian Message Stick Database if you agree. This alone can help reconnect them to their site of origin – in rare cases we've been able to do this by crossreferencing with sketches or photos in archives.     Piers  [19.06.2025:]  Dear Piers,    Thank you so much for your detailed reply.    I will pass on that information to my family, particularly my aunt Marjory, and if any more information emerges I will get back in touch.    We'd be very happy for you to add them to the database, that would be great.    Thanks again for sharing your knowledge.    With kind regards,    Ellen    [07.07.2025:]  Dear Piers,    This is a follow up regarding the Murchison incised message sticks that you had generously been helping me out with.     I am just sending through the known provenance information supplied but my aunt, Marjorie Glasson. Please find her short statement attached for your records.    I am hoping to place them either with WA Musuem or the Berndt Museum. I will let you know if/when they find a new home.      Bests,    Ellen    [attachment:]  The only connection that I know my family has had to the Murchison region is the family of Albert Hyden who went there in the late 1890s to work butchering on Meedo Station, at that time, owned by the Monger family.    The children of Albert Hyden were first cousins of Ruby Hyden, my mother and they knew each other as children.    The message sticks did belong to my mother and I can only surmise that the Hyden family gifted them to her when she was in her childhood.    I am in my late 80s and they were always in the house -kept in a drawer - where I grew up in Ararat. I don’t remember ever hearing them being talked about.     Marjorie Glasson  July 2025    [07.07.2025:]  Dear Ellen,  Thank you for sending this message through from Marjorie. I've added this detail to the Australian Message Stick Database and the revision will be live later in the year.   Do let me know if you manage to find a home for these objects.    Piers    [09.07.2025:]  Thanks for your reply, Piers. I'll stay in touch.    I have one other question to bother you with.     My friend, John Stanton in Perth (former Director at the Berndt Museum) is trying to locate an essay on the Murchison sticks which he believes is by the American professor, D.S. Davidson from the 30s.    Is that a piece of work you happen to be familiar with? Would you kindly let me know if there any thoughts on what they might be, and if not, no problem at all.    With thanks,    Ellen   [11.07.2025:]  Hi Ellen,  D. S. Davidson collected about 30 message sticks as part of his Australia expedition in 1931.   They seem to mostly be from Wardaman country in the NT and they now are at the Penn Museum.     I can't find any papers of his on message sticks, but that doesn't mean they don't exist. The nearest I have is a paper he contributed to that was written largely by Ethel Hassel and comments on message sticks used in the Noongar area. This is attached [Notes on the Ethnology of the Wheelman Tribe of Southwestern Australia].     If I come across anything else I'll let you know.    Piers    [28.01.2026:]  Dear Piers,    Just to let you know that the Murchison sticks we had discussed were received this week at the Western Australian Museum.    Anthropology head, Ross Chadwick, facilitated the donation.    Thanks again for your kind assistance with this matter.    Yours with thanks,    Ellen

title: A message stick from Rottnest-Wadjemup held in the Western Australian Museum
description:
WAM register: [Description] "MESSAGE STICK – 'boomerang'-shaped, cylindrical stick with curved arms; incised with frilly scratched lines forming a diamond pattern along body; old label [172] on one end and 'WA' in white mark on other end" 265 x 20mm. [Locality] Rottnest Island, WA; [Collector] Purchased and presented by Larry Foley, 58 Blackwell Reach Rd, Bicton WA 6000 [Date collected] 21 April, 1991 [Remarks] Purchased by collector at a Sotheby's Tribes Art auction for $935.00. The object was auctioned with the following story as documentation: "This message stick was sent from Rottnest Island in 1899 by a native named 'Cockroach'. It was given to a member of his tribe named "Mullet" who had served his term and was being sent back to his country.

The stick has to be handed to the tribal chief Googeerappa whose camp was at Black Hawke Bay, in the Flying Foam Pass, 20 miles from Cossack.

The stick was to warn Googerappa the 'Cockroach' was escaping, but was taken from Mullett by the Water Police. However, Cockroach escaped and returned to Foam Pass camp 9 months later. He was captured near Geraldton and returned to Fremantle. He was later sent back to Cossack where he died".

The collector subsequently presented the stick to the museum under the Taxation Incentives for the Arts School, 30.4.1994." [References] See File 0667

title: Messages stick from the Hann River region, Cape York
description:
Mjöberg, Eric. [1914] 2012. Among wild animals and people in Australia (Bland Vilda Djur och Folk i Australien). Translated by Margareta Luotsinen and Kim Akerman. Carlisle: Hesperian.: "During my expedition in the Kimberley I did not succeed in getting hold of any such message sticks. However during my second expedition in northern Queensland several of them fell into my hands. Even though this present book does not recount that trip, I cannot fail en passant to provide an example of such a message stick from Queensland, since it illustrates the natives' resourcefulness and ingenuity in a striking way. During my travels in the interior of Cape York Peninsula's more virgin districts, I suddenly came upon a Negro camp. Frightened at the sight of a caravan [157] of horses most of them fled with high screams, but some, who earlier had been in contact with a white man, and who knew a few words of pigeon English stayed. On the ground in front of them lay a newly carved message stick with inscriptions. I immediately confiscated the same and also succeeded in getting an explanation of the meaning of the inscription.

There was a lack of material for making spears in the camp. However a tribe further up on the Peninsula had a rich supply. A message was sent therefore to the north. A youth would bring over the friendly message stick, and spears along with other goods would be sent down as soon as circumstances permitted.

The message stick contained many facets. On one of its facets a number of long lines were seen. It was the number of spear shafts that they wished to get sent down; another side pictured graphically the number of young men who were to bring the trade material. Yet another asked for so and so many spear throwers or throwing sticks etc. A certain number of youths would meet the party coming from north – the path was on a facet marked by a zigzag line. This referred to the Hann River [fn:1: Hann River northeast Queensland – not to be confused with the Hann River in the Kimberley. KA.], which has a zigzag course. [PK: Note image in Endnote from Mjöberg’s 1918 book has four message sticks and the second from the left matches this description.]

In this way, simply but effectively, the children of the wilderness operate, when they wish to communicate with each other at a distance. The same system, although in different forms, seems to have a wide spread application over all parts of the continent. 158

PK: Note that the image is from a different book: Mjöberg, Eric. [1918] 2015. Amongst Stone Age people in the Queensland wilderness [Bland stenåldersmänniskor i Queenslands wildmarker]. Translated by S. M. Fryer. Carlisle, WA: Hesperian Press.

In this book he writes: "The carved hieroglyphics can be understood by the members of the new tribes and is a guarantee of the bearer's honesty. Sometimes the inscription on the stick carries a message. This was, without any doubt, the case with the stick, which I mentioned in my first book ( chapter 9, p. 251). On the surface could be seen a number of straight lines (Fig. 181). This indicated the number of spear shafts that a more southern tribe wished to obtain from a more northern tribe, in whose area a certain suitable plant grew. On the other side was indicated how many young men were needed to bring the material back. A zigzag line showed the route that they ought [266] to take. They were told to follow the Hann River, which twists and turns sharply to the left and to the right.

On other occasions the wooden stick acts more as a symbol that comes with a message from a different tribe, and the message itself is handed over by word of mouth. p267

title: A message stick purportedly from Rottnest-Wadjemup listed for sale on Live Auctioneers
description: Smalls auction description: "Rare Fine early Message Stick, Western Australia. Carved and engraved Message Stick made of wood with designs of lines and opposed triangles formed by punctured dots."
notes:
Sold by Smalls Auctions, Paddington NSW, on Live Auctioneers on 6 December 2025, Lot 0073.

Correspondence with auction house:

PK

Dec 03, 2025 12:16 PM GMT+11

Hello, I'm interested in this message stick but would need to know more about its history. The style appears to be similar to message sticks from the Murchison region of Western Australia. Does the private collector have any more particulars that they might be willing to share?

Smalls Auctions



Dec 04, 2025 9:39 AM GMT+11 Hi P, The Message Stick is from the Collection of Gene Van Grecken, now deceased. His son tells me that he has a recollection that it has a connection to Rottnest Island. Between 1838 and 1931, over 4,000 Aboriginal men and boys from across Western Australia were incarcerated on the island, so a displaced native from the Murchinson region may have well produced it. Smalls Auctions

PK Dec 04, 2025 6:13 PM GMT+11 Thank you for your response. I have, in fact, been researching message sticks from Rottnest Island on behalf of the Australian Museum including the names of the prisoners who sent them, the identities of the messengers and the content of the messages themselves. If Gene Van Grecken's son has any positive documentation linking this object to Rottnest Island, or an account of how the object entered into his father's collection, that would be very useful and I would be prepared to bid on the item. Smalls Auctions Dec 05, 2025 9:46 AM GMT+11

Hi P, Gene Van Grecken travelled through vast tracts of Central and Western Australia in the late 1940s, collecting Aboriginal Art and Artefacts, and this message stick was just one of hundreds of items he acquired. He didn't keep specific records of where he picked individual items up.

So, unfortunately, his son has no other information on this item except his recollection of what his father told him.

But, he tells me it is very similar to message sticks he's seen in the museum collections in the UK, which also purport to be from Rottnest Island, which I presume you have also studied.

Smalls Auctions

Thanks for letting me know.

There are many message sticks of this kind from the Murchison region, butmonly a very small number were made by prisoners on Rottnest. (There is only one Rottnest message stick is in the UK.) I will think about bidding on it, but it's probably too vague at this point. If the eventual buyer wants to get in touch with me after the auction, in order to contextualise this message stick, I can be contacted via a web search for the Australian Message Stick Project.

title: A message stick formerly on display at the Petrie Terrace Police Depot
description: Trove: "The Petrie Terrace Police Depot, Brisbane, is a museum of criminal relics connected with cases in the Queensland courts, and others which never have reached the stage of a trial. Humour as well as tragedy is represented. For instance, there is a small native "message stick," carved into the shape of a shield, about 6in. in length and half an inch in width, on which short marks had been cut, in a criss-cross manner, apparently with a stone knife. The marks were the equivalent of a written message, which, the attached not explained, was sent by a blackboy named Billy, of Gregory Downs, in 1894, to a gin on Lawn Hill. The message, according to the translation printed on the attached card, reads: "Dear Dora,— Send me a shirt and pair of trousers, and steal all you can from Mr. Hann." The Hann family, by the way, is one of the best known in Queensland grazing circles."

notes: 27.11.25 PK: Dear Queensland Police Museum,  I am the lead researcher on the Australian Message Stick Project: https://messagesticks.com.au/    I am writing to enquire about a message stick that was in the collection of the Petrie Terrace Police Depot Museum in 1933 and which I assume is now part of the Queensland Police Museum collection.    A 1933 article in the Queenslander Illustrated Weekly (http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article23266830) describes it in this way:    At the Petrie Terrace Police Depot, Brisbane, is a museum of criminal relics connected with cases in the Queensland courts, and others which never have reached the stage of a trial. Humour as well as tragedy is represented. For instance, there is a small native “message stick,” carved into the shape of a shield, about 6 in. in length and half an inch in width, on which short marks had been cut, in a criss-cross manner, apparently with a stone knife. The marks were the equivalent of a written message, which, the attached not explained, was sent by a blackboy named Billy, of Gregory Downs, in 1894, to a gin on Lawn Hill. The message, according to the translation printed on the attached card, reads: “Dear Dora,— Send me a shirt and pair of trousers, and steal all you can from Mr. Hann.”  The Hann family, by the way, is one of the best known in Queensland grazing circles.    Even if this artefact is no longer in your collection would you be able to provide any images of old registers or correspondence that indicates, for example,  how it was acquired, interpreted, displayed, exchanged or re-sold? I would also be grateful if you could provide any images of the artefact in question.    Many thanks,    Piers  01.12.2025:  Good morning Piers,    Thank you for your patience while I got back to you. We’ve received a few similar inquiries regarding our Collection.    When I joined the Museum four years ago, I found that there was very little documentation available, despite the collection dating back to 1893. Prior to my time, some correspondence from the State Archives mentioning objects or potential acquisitions for the Museum was photocopied. I’ve since digitised and indexed these records. However, the only reference we have to the message stick is the article you kindly shared in your email. I’ve attached our copy of the article for your reference.  Additionally, I’ve included a document from 1931 that confirms items in the Museum were described as being ‘scattered’. Although this document predates the article by two years, I believe this dispersal may explain how parts of the collection were lost over time. It’s also possible that further ‘scattering’ occurred in subsequent years.    The only photograph we have of the ‘old’ collection is from a 1933 newspaper clipping, which I’ve linked here: https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/198664746/21888332   Unfortunately, the article does not mention the message stick, and the photograph is not clear enough to confirm its presence. I’ve attached a higher-quality version of the clipping for your review, but I’m afraid it still doesn’t provide any definitive evidence of the message stick’s existence in the collection.    Unless further information comes to light, I am afraid I am unable to provide any answers to your questions.     If there’s anything else I can assist you with, please don’t hesitate to reach out.    Best regards,  K.F. (she/her)

Brammo Bay, Dunk Island.

[216] April 11/16.

Dear Doctor,

four blacks have, individually, promised to make message sticks, but so far—you know the foibles of the race—none is forthcoming. I note that you agree with views as to the illiteracy of the interesting folk, and that your investigation aims at producing evidence for and against. No doubt you have seen what Mrs. Aenas Gunn tells in her book "The Litte Black Princess" (p.57, for illustration) and may think that she makes out a good case: but when one listens to any black expounding such things there is little room for doubt that he is exercising his inventiveness to suit his audience, for if the sticks be taken from his and presented the next day it will be found to have quite a different version.

I got this bone myself on the site of the alleged tragedy, which is now in a banana clearing at the foot of Clump Point mountain. When the scrub was felled, quite recently, and burnt off the bones were calcined, save this, which I thought might interest you. The quests...

E. Banfield.

BRAMMO BAY, DUNK ISLAND, November 1906. 5

There came to our beach one afternoon some poor exiles from Princess Charlotte Bay—300 miles to the north. Exiled they felt themselves to be, and were longing to return to their own country, although their engagement for a six months’ cruise in quest of the passive bêche-de-mer had but just begun. One boy stepped along with an air of pride and importance. His companions were deferential to a certain extent, but they, too, exhibited an unusual demeanour. Some of the glory and honour that shone in Mattie’s face was reflected in theirs. With the assurance of an ambassador bearing high credentials he saluted me—

“Hello, Mister! Goodday.”

“Good day,” I responded. “You come from that cutter?”

Mattie—“Yes, mister. Mickie sit down here, now? Me got ‘em letter. Brother belonga gin, belonga Mickie; him gib it !”

“No; Mickie sit down alonga Palm Islands. Come back, bi’-mby.” [261]

Mattie (with a downcast air)—”My word! Bo’sun (the brother-in-law) gib it letter belonga Mickie.”

“Where letter?” I asked.

Mattie—"Me got ‘em,” and drawing out a very soiled little parcel, he proudly exposed a piece of greyish wood, about the size and shape of a lead pencil, on which had been cut two continuous intersecting grooves. “Me giv’ ‘em Mickie; Bo’sun alonga Cooktown. He want to come up this way now.”

The letter was a mere token of material expression of the fact that the sender was in the land of the living, and of his faith in the bearer, who was charged with all the personal messages and news. It was a sad rebuff to Mattie, elated with responsibility and eager to unburden himself of the latest domestic intelligence, to find that Mickie was not on the spot to receive it all. And, after fondling the wooden document for a while, he wrapped it up and carefully bestowed it within the bosom of his shirt. The disappointment was general. The gleam faded from the faces of the boys. For several days, first one and then another was entrusted with the honourable custody of the missive. Whoever possessed it for the time being was the most favoured individual. His worthiness for the office he acknowledged with an amusing air of self-consciousness and pride. Yours very truly and very hurriedly.

title: A message stick at the Ethnologisches Museum
description: EMB description: VI 2499 Keule, Stock oder Botenstab (?)  vor 1880 Eugen von Guérard, Sammler*in Australien  West-Australien Holz, geschnitzt 64,5 x 3 x 3 cm  0,3 kg
notes: 14.04.2026 PK: wrote to DD:  Dear DD,   I'm just reprising this dialogue from some years ago!    I visited your collection as a researcher in 2018 when I was just beginning to compile the Australian Message Stick Database, here: https://amsd.clld.org/  This database is now maintained from Australia, but the servers are in Göttingen, and the software is managed from Leipzig.     Thanks to your assistance in 2017-2018 I was able to add 34 message sticks from your collection to a database of now 2160 entries.     I'm preparing to visit Berlin again and I have two questions for you:  It's probably unlikely but are there now any more than 34 Australian message sticks currently in your collection? The technical term in German would be Botenstab, Botenstäbe, if you were to perform a search.  Adolf Bastian collected a spearthrower in 1881 or prior, that was repurposed as a message stick by a headman named Kaawirn Kuunawarn, also known as King Davie, or Hissing Swan. This object might never have been in your museum, but if it is, it might have been labelled as a spearthrower (Speerwerfer?) and not a message stick. It is one of the most significant message sticks ever recorded since it is the only one with a sign on it that represents a purely linguistic element. This, in part, inspired Bastian to write his 1881 article ,,Australische Schriftsubstitute." Here it is in the Australian Message Stick Database: https://amsd.clld.org/contributions/AB1881P192#4/-38.29/142.70 To see what it looks like, scroll to the bottom of that page and look at the image in the bottom right. Could you please do a search for objects collected by Bastian from Australia? Or search Australian spearthrowers? It's possible that it never left Australia and remained in the hands of James Dawson but was then lost in a fire. In any case I would like to rule out the possibility that it is with you in Berlin.  Many thanks! I can meet you in Berlin from 6-8 May or the following week, if that's more suitable.     All the best,  Piers    P.S. The research project has expanded a great deal since we first met. Here it is: https://messagesticks.com.au/    22.04.2026 DD:  Dear Piers,    Thank you very much for your email and the link to the database of message sticks. You’ve done a brilliant job. Congratulations.         Please accept my apologies for not replying sooner. I’m currently comparing your entries with ours in the database and will be in contact with you next week with a few questions.         I searched the database and found two sticks that were listed as “Stab” /stick in the catalogue, but as ‘Botenstab’ (?) on the index cards.    I have attached a list of these two items.         There is no object in the Bastian collection that corresponds to the drawing you mentioned.         All the best,    D    28.04.2026 PK:  Thank you DD!  And sorry for my own late reply. I'm in east Arnhem Land without regular access to the internet.     Thank you for sending these additional objects.     Some quick observations regarding their status as ,,fraglich":   VI 2499 has the appearance of a message stick even though it is unusually large. I can say more if you have a higher resolution photograph. The dating of 'before 1880' is also exceptionally early but not impossible. Most settlers didn't really know about message sticks as a concept until the late 1880s.   VI 8326 is more securely a message stick on the basis of the word 'Cundell'. This term is of uncertain origin but was used by Western Australian settlers for 'message stick' up until the 1920s. It's possibly from a southwest language, and would be spelled kurntal, or similar, today.  I haven't yet been able to track it down but I'm working on it with linguist Troy Reynolds. Before 1887 is also quite early so this would be an important object for understanding the practice in southwest Western Australia.     Let me know how you go with your comparisons.    I expect to get to Berlin on Tuesday next week. If you have time for lunch or a coffee let me know. I can take a break from the conference at Petri to say hello.    PK
